blocks.content: A semaphore is a synchronization primitive built around a single integer counter. Threads coordinate access to shared resources purely by manipulating that counter through two atomic operations. It is one of the oldest and most versatile tools in concurrent programming, and still a fixture of operating systems interviews.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416992-99154776.png
1. What Is a Semaphore

A semaphore is an integer counter that is never touched directly. The only way to change it is through two atomic operations: wait, also called P or down, and signal, also called V or up. Because both operations are atomic, no two threads can corrupt the counter by modifying it at the same time.

wait checks the counter. If it is greater than zero, it decrements the counter and the thread proceeds immediately. If decrementing would take the counter below zero, the thread instead blocks and joins a waiting queue. signal increments the counter, and if any thread is waiting, one of them is woken up and allowed to proceed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416993-914750214.png

blocks.title: The counter is the whole mechanism
blocks.content: Everything a semaphore does reduces to this one counter and the two atomic operations that touch it. There is no hidden state, no owner, and no extra bookkeeping beyond the integer itself.
2. Binary Semaphore

A binary semaphore restricts its counter to only two values, 0 and 1. Initialized to 1, it behaves like a simple lock: a thread calls wait to bring the counter to 0 and enter, then calls signal to bring it back to 1 and let the next thread in.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416993-535063920.png

On the surface this looks identical to a mutex, and for the simple case of one lock protecting one resource it behaves the same way. The real differences only show up once ownership and intent are examined, covered in section 4.
3. Counting Semaphore

A counting semaphore allows its counter to be any non negative integer, not just 0 or 1. It is initialized to the number of identical, interchangeable resources available, and every wait call hands out one unit while every signal call returns one.

Picture a connection pool with exactly three identical database connections. A counting semaphore initialized to 3 lets the first three threads through immediately, each decrementing the counter by one. A fourth thread that arrives while the counter is at 0 blocks until an earlier thread finishes and signals.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416993-333777096.png
4. Semaphore vs Mutex

This distinction is one of the most common operating systems interview questions, and the confusion almost always starts because a binary semaphore looks so similar to a mutex on the surface. Two properties actually separate them: ownership and purpose.

{"headers":["Aspect","Mutex","Semaphore"],"rows":[["Ownership","Owned by the thread that locked it, typically only that thread can unlock it","No ownership concept, any thread can call signal, even one that never called wait"],["Value range","Effectively binary, locked or unlocked","Binary semaphore is 0 or 1, counting semaphore is any non negative integer"],["Purpose","Mutual exclusion for exactly one resource","Managing access to a pool of N identical resources, or general signaling between threads"],["Typical use","Protecting a single shared data structure","Bounded buffers, connection pools, signaling between producer and consumer"]]}
4.1 Ownership

A mutex has a strict notion of ownership. The thread that calls lock is the only thread allowed to call unlock, and most implementations throw an error or produce undefined behavior if a different thread tries to release it.

A semaphore has no such rule. Any thread can call signal on a semaphore, including a thread that never called wait on it at all. This is not a bug, it is intentional, and it is exactly what makes semaphores useful for signaling between different threads rather than only for locking.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416993-599697026.png
4.2 Purpose

A mutex exists to guard exactly one resource so that only one thread touches it at a time. A semaphore, especially a counting semaphore, exists to manage access to a pool of N interchangeable resources, or to signal events between threads that have nothing to do with locking.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416993-351628970.png

If you only remember one line for the interview: a mutex is about ownership of one resource, a semaphore is a counter with no ownership that can manage many resources or simply pass signals between threads.
5. Worked Example: A Pool of Three Printers
blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: A Pool of Three Printers

blocks.content: Suppose an office has exactly three identical printers, modeled with a counting semaphore initialized to 3. Four threads request a printer at roughly the same time, and tracing the counter makes the mechanism concrete.

["Thread A calls wait. Counter drops from 3 to 2, and A starts printing immediately.","Thread B calls wait. Counter drops from 2 to 1, and B starts printing immediately.","Thread C calls wait. Counter drops from 1 to 0, and C starts printing immediately.","Thread D calls wait. The counter is already 0, so D blocks and joins the waiting queue.","Thread A finishes and calls signal. Counter rises from 0 to 1, and D is woken up and given the printer."]
items: Thread A calls wait. Counter drops from 3 to 2, and A starts printing immediately.
Thread B calls wait. Counter drops from 2 to 1, and B starts printing immediately.
Thread C calls wait. Counter drops from 1 to 0, and C starts printing immediately.
Thread D calls wait. The counter is already 0, so D blocks and joins the waiting queue.
Thread A finishes and calls signal. Counter rises from 0 to 1, and D is woken up and given the printer.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416994-579177063.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: A Pool of Three Printers

blocks.content: The counter never needs to track all four threads at once, it only tracks how many printers are currently free. That single number is enough to correctly admit exactly three threads and queue the rest.
6. Producer Consumer Preview

The producer consumer problem is the canonical example of what semaphores are built for. Producers generate items into a bounded buffer and consumers remove them, and two counting semaphores keep both sides honest.

empty starts at the buffer capacity and tracks free slots, decremented by producers and incremented by consumers. full starts at 0 and tracks filled slots, incremented by producers and decremented by consumers. Together they block producers when the buffer is full and block consumers when it is empty.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408416994-881892107.png

blocks.title: Its own dedicated topic
blocks.content: This is only a preview to show why semaphores matter. The full producer consumer problem, including the buffer mutex needed alongside empty and full, gets its own dedicated topic.
7. Common Mistakes
Two mistakes account for most semaphore bugs in practice, and both are worth watching for explicitly.
7.1 Signal without a matching wait

Calling signal without a corresponding prior wait increments the counter beyond what the actual resource pool supports. The semaphore then believes more units are free than truly exist, and a later thread can be let through to a resource that is not actually available.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558638-313081713.png
7.2 Using a semaphore where a mutex was the right tool
blocks.text: 7.2 Using a semaphore where a mutex was the right tool

blocks.content: When there is exactly one resource and mutual exclusion with clear ownership is all that is needed, a mutex is the simpler and safer choice. Reaching for a binary semaphore instead works on the surface but throws away ownership checking, making it easier for a thread to accidentally release a lock it never held.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408558640-374667879.png
blocks.alt: Using a semaphore where a mutex was the right tool

blocks.content: 8. Interview Angle

When asked to compare a mutex and a semaphore, lead with ownership, since that is the property that actually distinguishes them once the counter is restricted to 0 and 1. Follow with purpose: mutual exclusion for one resource versus managing a pool of N resources or signaling between threads.

blocks.title: Quick recall check
blocks.content: Mutex: owned by the locking thread, only that thread can unlock it, protects one resource. Semaphore: no ownership, any thread can signal, a counting semaphore manages a pool of N resources, and two semaphores together can coordinate producers and consumers.
